verdicts.conflict: Whether artificial intelligence functions primarily as a productivity ratchet that intensifies labor demands without reducing working hours.
verdicts.rationale: Both sides present valid empirical counterpoints without settling the broader systemic question. The accelerationist camp cites hard deployment data from Klarna handling two-thirds of chats, while the skeptic camp notes that ticket containment numbers ignore uncounted human escalation channels. Without longitudinal data tracking total labor hours and error resolution across both automated and manual channels, neither argument decisively proves its case.
verdicts.whatWouldChange: Comprehensive longitudinal time-use studies tracking both automated ticket containment and downstream escalation workloads across multiple enterprise deployments.

verdicts.conflict: Whether eliminating manual sign-off layers generates genuine productivity gains or merely shifts validation debt onto downstream teams.
verdicts.rationale: The accelerationist position offers specific post-automation exception ratio drops of thirty-five percent over six months. Conversely, the skeptic position highlights the transfer of cognitive burden onto frontline workers when review gates disappear. The debate remains balanced because specific error reductions in one metric do not rule out the transfer of cognitive burdens to unmeasured escalation paths.
verdicts.whatWouldChange: Audits of frontline employee error-correction frequency and cognitive load metrics following the removal of front-end review gates.
